headline: Scientists Reverse Aging Signs in Mice by Restoring Brain Protein
meta_description: Researchers found that restoring Menin, a declining brain protein, reversed age-related changes in mice including bone loss, skin thinning, and cognitive decli…
summary_short: A brain protein called Menin appears to drive aging. When scientists restored it in older mice, several signs of aging reversed—stronger bones, thicker skin, and better…
body:
A brain protein called Menin may hold a key to aging itself. When scientists at Xiamen University restored this protein in elderly mice, they reversed multiple signs of aging: the animals' bones became stronger, their skin thickened, and their cognitive abilities improved. The findings suggest that declining Menin levels, which occur naturally with age in specific brain cells, may be one of the driving forces behind the body's gradual decline. Importantly, these improvements appeared within thirty days of treatment, offering a glimpse of how quickly aging-related damage might respond to intervention.

The research centered on the hypothalamus, a small but powerful brain region that coordinates metabolism and influences how the body ages. Scientists discovered that as mice grew older, Menin levels fell specifically in neurons within the ventromedial hypothalamus—a drop that didn't occur in other brain cell types. When the team reduced Menin in younger mice, age-related traits emerged: inflammation increased, bone mass decreased, skin thinned, and cognitive abilities declined. Reversing the process by delivering the Menin gene into the hypothalamus of 20-month-old mice reversed these changes and extended lifespan.

Beyond Menin itself, the research uncovered a connection to D-serine, an amino acid essential for learning and memory. Mice with less Menin had lower D-serine levels, and treating mice with D-serine improved their cognitive performance. However, the amino acid alone didn't reproduce the full anti-aging effects seen with Menin restoration—a distinction that matters as researchers explore how these findings might translate to human health. The work suggests that aging may be driven not by one inevitable decline, but by specific molecular shifts that, in principle, could be addressed.
quick_facts: Study led by scientists at Xiamen University in China
Tested in elderly mice aged 20 months old
Improvements in bone mass, skin thickness, and cognition appeared within 30 days
Menin loss linked to inflammation, bone weakness, skin thinning, and memory problems
Research published in journal PLOS Biology in March 2023
